outcome: Nothing found since 26 Jan 2024 that settles, or moves a quantity in, the question of whether infinitely many Pierpont primes exist: the only in-window items are a computational list extension (OEIS A374577, July to September 2024) and a neighbouring OpenAI manuscript (dated 24 Sep 2026) on primes whose predecessor is smooth with a smoothness bound that grows with x; the problem is still listed as open.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many Pierpont primes? The statement does not define the term, so the standard definition is used (Wikipedia, OEIS A005109, Guy's Unsolved Problems in Number Theory): a Pierpont prime is a prime of the form 2^u * 3^v + 1 with u and v nonnegative integers, equivalently a prime p whose p - 1 has no prime factor other than 2 and 3. Parts of the question: (a) the set of such primes is infinite. Not asked by the statement: counts or asymptotics of Pierpont primes (for example Gleason's roughly 9n up to 10^n heuristic), the full list, or the second-kind primes 2^u * 3^v - 1.

events.what_happened: Andrew M. Gleason, 'Angle trisection, the heptagon, and the triskaidecagon', Amer. Math. Monthly 95(3) (1988), pp. 185-194, is the standard citation for the constructibility criterion (regular n-gon constructible with ruler, compass and angle trisector iff n = 2^r 3^s times distinct Pierpont primes greater than 3). Wikipedia's Pierpont prime article attributes to Gleason an explicit probabilistic heuristic: among n-digit numbers of the form 2^u 3^v + 1 the chance of primality is about 1/n, so there are Theta(n) Pierpont primes among Theta(n^2) candidates; Gleason is said to have conjectured infinitely many, with about 9n Pierpont primes up to 10^n. The 1988 paper itself was not read (the JSTOR page returned an error), so whether the heuristic or the infinitude conjecture is stated there, rather than in later literature, is not established. The t5k glossary cites the same paper only for the constructibility result and does not state the heuristic.
events.delivers: A heuristic, not a theorem: a counting prediction that the Pierpont primes are infinite and number about 9n up to 10^n. Establishes no instance and no infinitude.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the infinitude is conjectured by the heuristic and is not proved.
events.direction: Predicts that the Pierpont primes are infinite, so it points the way the question asks; it is a heuristic and proves nothing either way.

events.what_happened: William D. Banks, Asma Harcharras and Igor E. Shparlinski, 'Smooth values of shifted primes in arithmetic progressions', Michigan Math. J. 52(3) (Dec 2004), pp. 603-618, DOI 10.1307/mmj/1100623415. The Project Euclid page gave metadata only (full text is paywalled). From the title, the search summaries and the Naccache-Shparlinski survey (arXiv 0810.2067, abstract read; the survey's body was not readable), this is a line of work bounding counts of primes p up to x with p - h y-smooth, for a fixed nonzero h. The paper's theorem statements and exact ranges were not read; the survey's claims about upper bounds and the difficulty of lower bounds come from a search summary, not from the paper.
events.delivers: Per the search summaries, upper-bound estimates for counts of primes whose shifted value p - h is y-smooth, for smoothness parameters y that grow with x (exact range not read). This is a counting bound for a different smoothness regime, not 3-smooth p - 1. An upper bound on a count cannot give infinitude.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the result does not concern the case y = 3 and gives no lower bound.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed mathematics journal publishing the paper in 2004
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, Vol. 52, No. 3, pp. 603-618

events.direction: Neighbouring result: counts of primes with a shifted value smooth for a growing smoothness bound. It runs in the upper-bound direction and says nothing about whether 3-smooth p - 1 occurs infinitely often.

events.what_happened: OEIS A234361 (entry by Zhi-Wei Sun, dated 24 Dec 2013) defines a(n) as the number of k in 0 < k < n with 2^(phi(k)/2) 3^(phi(n-k)/4) + 1 prime, where phi is Euler's totient function. The entry states 'Conjecture: a(n) > 0 for all n > 7' and 'This implies that there are infinitely many primes of the form 2^k*3^m + 1, where k and m are positive integers.' The entry links only to a b-file of terms n = 1 to 5000. This is a conjecture with a stated implication, not a result.
events.revisions: OEIS page last modified 11 Oct 2026 (page date; revision history not inspected).
events.delivers: Nothing proved. If the conjecture a(n) > 0 for all n > 7 holds, it would imply infinitely many primes 2^k 3^m + 1 with k, m positive, which is the infinitude of a Pierpont-type family. The entry does not claim the implication is established.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the conjecture itself is open, and the implication runs only one way.
events.directly_checkable: The counts a(n) for given n are explicit computations and the b-file gives values to n = 5000; but the conjecture quantifies over all n, so finite checks do not settle it.
events.direction: A conjecture that would imply the problem's claim if true; it asserts nothing decided.

events.what_happened: Jori Merikoski, 'On the largest square divisor of shifted primes', arXiv 1907.02246 (first submitted 4 July 2019; v3 notes small corrections after referee comments), published in Acta Arithmetica 196 (2020), pp. 349-386 (journal details from a search result, not opened). Shows infinitely many primes p such that p - 1 is divisible by a square d^2 at least p^(1/2 + 1/2000). The abstract page was read; the full text was not.
events.revisions: v1 4 Jul 2019; v3 with small corrections after referee comments (per arXiv comment field).
events.delivers: Infinitely many primes p with p - 1 divisible by a square d^2 >= p^(1/2 + 1/2000). A divisibility property of p - 1, not a smoothness property: it neither gives nor rules out p - 1 being 3-smooth.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the result concerns a different property of p - 1.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in vol. 196 (2020), pp. 349-386

events.direction: Neighbouring result on square divisors of shifted primes; does not bear on whether 3-smooth p - 1 occurs infinitely often.

events.what_happened: PrimePages (t5k.org) records that 81 * 2^20498148 + 1 (6,170,560 decimal digits) was proved prime; the submission is dated 13 June 2023 (log: 6/13/2023 12:33:12 UTC). The primality proof is an N-1 test (Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge) run in PFGW, elapsed time 3.65 days; the proof code is credited to Propper with LLR. Wikipedia's Pierpont prime article gives the same term as the largest known Pierpont prime, dated 'as of 2023', and says its primality was discovered in June 2023. The number has the form 2^u 3^v + 1 with u = 20498148 and v = 4 (81 = 3^4).
events.delivers: One further instance of the form 2^u 3^v + 1. It adds one Pierpont prime to the list and moves no quantity the question asks about, since the problem asks whether the list is infinite, not how long it is.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: finitely many instances, however large, do not decide infinitude.

events.what_happened: OEIS A374577 (entry by William C. Laursen, 11 Jul 2024) lists the exponents t of 2 in the Pierpont primes 2^t 3^u + 1, in increasing order of the primes; more terms were added by Stefano Spezia on 12 Jul 2024; Mathematica and PARI programs were added by Amiram Eldar on 2 Sep 2024. The companion A374578 gives the exponents of 3. The entry extends a table of known Pierpont primes and states no infinitude claim.

events.delivers: Lists further known instances of Pierpont primes computed from a table. It adds instances and nothing about infinitude.
events.directly_checkable: Each listed prime is explicit and can be checked with a primality test; the list is finite.
events.direction: Extends the finite list of instances; points neither way on whether the list is infinite.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, 'An average Brun-Titchmarsh theorem and shifted primes with a large prime factor', arXiv 2508.18285 (first submitted 19 Aug 2025; later versions around 7 Oct 2025). The abstract page was read: it says that for infinitely many primes p the largest prime factor of p - 1 exceeds p^0.679 (the main theorem carries an epsilon loss), improving the exponent 0.677 of Baker and Harman (1998). The full paper was not read.
events.revisions: v1 19 Aug 2025; later versions around 7 Oct 2025 (per search summary; arXiv listing not opened for version history).
events.delivers: Infinitely many primes p with p - 1 having a prime factor above p^0.679. This is the opposite extreme from smoothness: such p - 1 are not 3-smooth, so the result says nothing about whether 3-smooth p - 1 occur infinitely often.
events.direction: Neighbouring result about large prime factors of p - 1; points the opposite way from smoothness and does not bear on the question.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, 'Largest square divisors of shifted primes', arXiv 2505.23779 (v1 16 May 2025; v2 17 Oct 2025). The abstract page was read: infinitely many primes p such that, for any nonzero integer a, p - a is divisible by a square d^2 > p^(1/2 + 1/700), improving Merikoski's exponent 1/2 + 1/2000. The full paper was not read.
events.delivers: Square divisors of p - a for all nonzero a. A divisibility property, not smoothness: it neither gives nor rules out 3-smooth p - 1.
events.direction: Neighbouring result on square divisors of shifted primes; does not bear on 3-smooth p - 1.

events.what_happened: An OpenAI manuscript titled 'Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers' (Family 011 of the openai/math collection; the family title is 'Prime-factor statistics of p-1'). Its date, 24 Sep 2026, comes from a third-party repository (daizisheng/erdos-824) that relies on it; the PDF was not read, and the description below comes from a search summary of the Pitt catalogue (not opened: the page was too large to fetch) and from that repository. Claimed content, as described: a resolution of an Erdos conjecture on the largest fibres of Euler's totient, and, for every fixed delta > 0, at least x^(1 - o(1)) primes p in (2x, 5x] whose predecessor p - 1 has no prime factor exceeding x^delta. The third-party repository states that its Theorem 2 is conditional on this manuscript and that Sections 3-5 of the manuscript 'have not been independently verified'.
events.revisions: Not established; catalogue status as of 7 Oct 2026 per search summary.
events.delivers: A lower bound on the number of primes p whose p - 1 is x^delta-smooth, with the smoothness bound growing with x. This is a different quantity from 3-smooth p - 1: the smoothness parameter is not fixed at 3, and the result gives no infinitude for the 3-smooth family.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the 3-smooth family is not treated.
events.doubts: Unrefereed 2026 manuscript. The only public engagement found is a third-party repository (Shisheng Li and Zhong Zhuang, Erdos problem 824) that builds a conditional Theorem 2 on it and says Sections 3-5 'have not been independently verified'. Whether the manuscript has a Lean formalisation is not established: a search summary reports that it was not listed in the Pitt catalogue's Lean scope notes.
events.direction: Neighbouring result on smooth shifted primes with a smoothness bound that grows with x. It cuts nowhere on the 3-smooth question as stated.

disputes.summary: Wikipedia credits Gleason with the counting heuristic of about 9n Pierpont primes up to 10^n and with the conjecture of infinitude, citing his 1988 Monthly paper. The t5k glossary cites the same paper only for the constructibility criterion and does not state the heuristic. A search summary of Cox and Shurman (Monthly, 2005) reports that Gleason suggested there may be infinitely many Pierpont primes; that PDF was unreadable, so the claim is unverified. Not resolved here.

summary: Nothing in the window settles, or moves a quantity in, the question. The problem is still open: the Wikipedia Pierpont prime article says 'It has been conjectured that there are infinitely many Pierpont primes, but this remains unproven' (its last edit is dated 29 June 2026 per the fetched page; the infobox says 'As of 2023'), and the current unsolved-problems list still carries the bullet 'Are there infinitely many Pierpont primes?'. No opened source reports a proof, disproof, conditional theorem, or Pierpont-specific partial result after 26 January 2024. The t5k glossary states the usual contrast: simple heuristics suggest finitely many Fermat primes (v = 0) but infinitely many Pierpont primes. Counts are heuristic-supported: Wikipedia gives 42 below 10^6, 65 below 10^9, 157 below 10^20 and 795 below 10^100, and the t5k table gives 4227 below 10^512. The in-window items are a list extension (OEIS A374577, July to Sept 2024), which adds instances only, and a neighbouring OpenAI manuscript (dated 24 Sep 2026 by a third-party repository; PDF unread) on primes whose p - 1 has no prime factor above x^delta, a smoothness bound that grows with x. The largest known term, 81 * 2^20498148 + 1, was proved prime in June 2023 (before the window) and is one more instance. The other neighbours are about different properties of p - 1: Li 2025 (large prime factor above p^0.679, which implies only that infinitely many p - 1 are not 3-smooth), Li 2025 and Merikoski 2019 (square divisors), and Banks, Harcharras and Shparlinski 2004 (upper bounds for counts with growing smoothness; paywalled, metadata only). OEIS A234361 (Sun, Dec 2013) conjectures a(n) > 0 for n > 7, which would imply infinitude if true; it is a conjecture. Close calls: (i) the OpenAI manuscript's title says 'smooth shifted primes', so a keyword reader could count it as partial progress; I read it as a different quantity because its smoothness bound is not fixed at 3. (ii) Gleason's roughly 9n heuristic is strong evidence for the conjecture but is not a result, and its attribution to the 1988 paper is unverified. (iii) Each Pierpont prime found is an instance, which under the scope rule moves nothing. AI: no opened source credits an AI system with any Pierpont-specific mathematics. The AI-term searches (Pierpont with GPT, Claude, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof; Erdos problems and AI; Lean/mathlib; 2026 announcements) found nothing on Pierpont primes, and I read the openai/math CONTENTS.md in full: none of its titles mentions Pierpont, 3-smooth numbers or 2^a 3^b. The only AI-attributed event is the OpenAI family-011 manuscript, with the lab's collection README as the basis (not the manuscript text). The README says 719 manuscripts in 372 families; press coverage says 722; I could not resolve the discrepancy. Press reports of about three hours of ChatGPT Pro compute per result and a 'single prompt, single agent' statement are not authors' accounts, so they are not recorded as cost or basis. The Sawhney and Sellke disclosures (Sept 2026) and the Axiom 246-gap formalisation concern other problems according to search summaries; I did not open them. Erdos Problem 1065 asks about p = 2^k q + 1 and 2^k 3^l q + 1 with q prime; q = 1 is excluded, so it is a neighbour rather than this problem, and its page gave no status and no readable forum text. Pierpont's own 1895 paper introduced the primes for the constructibility question and says nothing on infinitude; it is background and not recorded as an event.
competing_reading: The strongest case for weighing the evidence differently: the Gleason-style count (about 1/log x per candidate over about (log x)^2 pairs (u, v) with 2^u 3^v below x, giving a divergent expected count) plus steady new record primes make infinitude very likely, and a reader who treats 'very likely infinite' as progress could weigh the 2023 instance and the 2026 OpenAI manuscript as movement. Under the scope rule neither changes the question. The narrower competing reading of the OpenAI manuscript is that if its argument extended to a fixed smoothness bound, its count would bear on the problem; as described it does not, because its bound x^delta grows with x. This depends on the manuscript text, which I did not read.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The OpenAI manuscript 'Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers' (PDF in openai/math under family 011): whether any theorem gives a smoothness bound fixed independently of x, in particular 3-smooth p - 1, and whether it has a Lean formalisation. (2) Gleason's 1988 Monthly paper (JSTOR 2323624): whether it states the infinitude conjecture and the 9n count. (3) A full-text arXiv search for 'Pierpont' and '3-smooth' (the arXiv search results only matched titles or abstracts and returned one unrelated 2013 paper). (4) The Wikipedia article's revision history after 2023, for any post-2023 record or claim. (5) A GitHub code search for 'Pierpont' in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures and mathlib; GitHub code search requires login here, so it was not run.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many primes 2^u 3^v + 1 exist. No event proves or bounds that. Two events are lists of instances: the 2023 record prime and the 2024 OEIS list extension. Gleason's heuristic and Sun's conjecture prove nothing, so they are none. The smooth-shifted-prime, large-prime-factor and square-divisor results each settle a different question about p - 1, so they are variant. The close call was the OpenAI manuscript. Its x^delta smoothness bound grows with x, so its count cannot give infinitely many 3-smooth p - 1, and it is a variant. I marked its AI role generated because the lab's README says the manuscript was produced by its model. That has no effect on this problem, because the event is discarded.
judgement.doubts: The OpenAI manuscript was not read; if it contained a fixed-smoothness theorem the reading would change, but nothing in the record suggests it does. Its AI attribution rests on the collection-level README, not the manuscript itself.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
